newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Army orders Sierra Leoneans back to work.
newsitem.headline: Army orders Sierra Leoneans back to work.

text.p: Workers in Sierra Leone turned up outside their offices on Monday after the new army rulers ordered them to return to work or face the sack.

But the workers, who have stayed away for two weeks since the coup, stood outside on the pavements saying they were reluctant to go back as they had not been paid their May salaries and soldiers were still looting what little equipment remained in their offices.
"Last night the army looted the few remaining electric fans," said a clerk at the Freetown magistrates' court.
Hundreds of shoppers descended on three groceries which opened downtown, to stock up on rice, sugar and flour. Heavily armed soldiers guarded shops to prevent fights breaking out.
"Since I've been in Sierra Leone I've never sold as much as this morning." said Lebanese trader Ibrahim Bazzy.
He said shops' stocks were running out and there was no immediate prospect of restocking as Lebanese importers had fled the country after the coup.
A senior harbour official said several boats carrying rice and other foodstuffs which were expected this week had been diverted to neighbouring Guinea where many importers now were.
Rumours spread that Nigeria was planning an air strike following its unsuccessful intervention a week ago. Churches and mosques in the city have been holding prayer sessions for peace.

Nigeria has been building up its forces in Freetown, but has lost the use of Hastings airport on the eastern outskirts of the city, creating logistical problems for any ground-based strike to force the restoration of the elected government.
The central bank was burned down in the coup and the leone currency, which was rising against the dollar before the May 25 takeover has fallen from 860 to the dollar to more than 1,000.
The military authorities confirmed on Monday that the International Monetary Fund had suspended its funding following the coup.
People are still fleeing Freetown for the interior and hundreds are sleeping in the open air at the docks hoping to find a boat to take them out of the country.
The military authorities, who have promised to crack down on looting, put piles of stolen electronic goods on display at military headquarters and invited people to come and claim their property.

Workers have stayed home during the coup, which has been condemned at home and abroad, but a statement repeatedly broadcast on Sierra Leone radio since Saturday has warned that anyone absent from work without a valid reason would be sacked.
"Workers in Sierra Leone are, therefore, warned that any further failure to perform their duties to their employers would result to summary dismissal," a statement said.
"With the supply of surplus labour in the country, replacement could be easily secured."
The new military rulers have sent delegations to West African countries to explain the reasons for their coup, which ousted a 14-month-old elected government.
A delegation met Ivory Coast's president Henri Konan Bedie on Sunday and was planning to travel on to Ghana.
